title: American Eel
summary: The American eel connects Long Island waterways with Shinnecock fishing knowledge and finely woven eel pots.
content:
A life linking fresh and salt water

The American eel (Anguilla rostrata) uses estuaries and inland waters during its life and returns to the Atlantic’s Sargasso Sea to reproduce. NYSDEC highlights it as a fish connecting freshwater habitat with the ocean. Its long body moves through water with a wave-like motion.[1]

Fishing in Shinnecock memory

The Shinnecock Environmental Department’s 2014 catalogue records Elders’ memories of winter eel fishing in Heady Creek. Their recollections connect community foodways with seasonal knowledge and changes in the waterway around the 1938 hurricane.[2]

The skill in an eel pot

The National Museum of the American Indian catalogues a Shinnecock eel pot from Long Island, dated about 1890. Made from oak splints and wood using wicker plaiting, it preserves an example of the close relationship between fishing and basketmaking. The maker is not named in the museum record.[3]

Connected waters

An eel’s life invites us to follow connections between creeks, bays, and the sea. How might a change in one part of that system affect the rest? The map illustration swims within bay water; it does not show an individual eel’s migration or a fishing location.

References

  1. NYSDEC, Offshore Ocean Habitats and Inshore Estuarine Habitats
  2. Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders (2014), animal entries. Project research archive.
  3. National Museum of the American Indian, Shinnecock eel trap/pot, catalogue 7/3508
why_this_matters: An eel links inland water, coastal bays, and the ocean. Shinnecock fishing knowledge and woven eel pots reveal the skill involved in understanding those connected waters.
